ending_first.ending: That night Maren dates a photograph, files it with a railing bolt and a bagged shoe in a fifth identical box, and shelves the box beside four others while Derek sleeps in the chair and tells her she does not sleep; the person who went over is never found and Coastguard never arrives inside the day.
ending_first.cost: Another unofficial archive of a person the tide has already taken, and another night she will not sleep.
ending_first.final_image: A closed shoebox set on the shelf beside four identical boxes, under tide charts, one now marked in red.

jacket_copy: Before dawn a harbour watchkeeper walks the east wall in waterproofs over a nightdress. The railing is bent outward. Paint comes away wet on her fingers. She radios the station: somebody went over. The torch finds nothing on the black water. Coastguard cannot put a boat out for four hours. Four hours is the whole tide. Derek Algood already knows what four hours is. In the station office he stands with his coat still on and argues the time of entry. She traces a line on the annotated charts, takes a key off the board, and does not take her coat off either. They launch themselves. At the harbour mouth the bar is a white line of broken water. He tells her this is not a search. She turns the wheel anyway, toward a stretch of grey sand nobody stands on twice.
plot_summary_short: Tideline is a short contemporary drama set at a working harbour in the coastal present. Harbour-station watchkeeper Maren Vosk, a woman in her fifties, finds the east-wall railing bent outward before dawn and the paint still wet, which she treats as proof that someone has gone over into the water. Coastguard procedure will not put a boat out for four hours, and four hours is a full tide that closes the search window. Her younger colleague Derek Algood reports the delay and argues that she cannot know when the person entered the water. Maren traces the tide charts, takes the station-boat key from the board, and launches herself with Derek riding along. At the harbour mouth he tells her this is not a search; she turns the wheel across the bar, a line of broken water, anyway. On a sandbar that local rule says nobody stands on twice, she finds a shoe, replaces it exactly where it lay, marks the spot, and photographs it. That night, while Derek sleeps in a station chair and tells her she does not sleep, she dates the photograph, puts it in a shoebox with a railing bolt and the bagged shoe, and shelves the box beside four identical unofficial archives. The missing person is not recovered.
plot_summary_long:
Tideline is a short contemporary realist drama with a thin mystery line, set at a working harbour in the coastal present. The story follows Maren Vosk, a harbour-station watchkeeper in her fifties, who finds evidence that someone has gone over the east wall before dawn and tries to search for them inside a tide window that official rescue will not meet. A harbour-station watchkeeper is the person on duty at the small office that keeps tide records, a radio, and a station boat; her job is to walk the walls, report, and hold the watch, not to run a coastguard rescue. The plot turns on a few operational rules. Tides here run on a clock no one can delay, and four hours is a full tide, which means the water will have moved any person past the useful ground and closed the search window. Coastguard, the official sea-rescue service, cannot put a boat out in under four hours, so an official launch will always arrive after this tide is spent. The station keeps its own small launch, started with a key hung on a board in the office; taking that key is unsanctioned but physically open to anyone on the watch. Wet paint on a railing bent outward is treated inside this station as a reliable recent stamp that a body went over. At the harbour mouth a bar of broken water must be crossed to reach open ground. Beyond it, at low water, a sandbar is exposed; local practice is that nobody stands on that sand twice. The station also keeps unofficial physical archives, ordinary identical boxes of objects from prior losses, that the official search will not keep. The person who went over is never named and never shown. The story runs on two crossing lines: Maren's insistence that a missing person is still searchable, and Derek's insistence, backed by the tide clock and Coastguard delay, that the search is already over. They share the station and the watch, so neither can simply leave the other.

Before dawn, under wind and a single sodium lamp, Maren walks the east harbour wall in waterproofs worn over a nightdress, carrying a torch. The water is black and moving. She stops where the railing is bent outward, crouches, and puts two fingers on the paint. The paint comes away wet. She radios the station on a handheld set, identifies herself as Vosk at the east wall, and reports that the railing is gone and that somebody went over. A voice on the radio tells her to go ahead and uses her first name. She sweeps the torch across the water and finds nothing.

At dawn she enters the harbour-station office, lit by fluorescent tubes, where a wall of tide charts is annotated in three different hands. Derek Algood, a colleague about thirty, stands with his coat still on and reports Coastguard's four-hour minimum before they can get a boat out. Maren answers that four hours is the whole tide. Derek says he knows what four hours is. She goes to the charts, traces a line with one finger from west to east, and states that if the person went in at three they are already past the bar. Derek objects that she does not know they went in at three. She answers that the paint was wet. He looks at the floor, then at her boots, which are also wet, and asks how long she was out there. She does not answer. She takes a key off the board and leaves without removing her coat. Derek goes with her.

In the morning they are in the station launch at the harbour mouth, in diesel and spray. Maren is at the wheel. Derek rides in the bow holding a boat hook he does not use. He tells her this is not a search and that she knows it. She answers that it is a search until somebody tells her it is not. The boat crests. Ahead the bar shows as a white line of broken water. Derek says her name as a warning. She says she knows. She turns the wheel anyway and crosses the bar.

At low water they reach the sandbar, a stretch of grey sand the local rule says nobody stands on twice. Maren walks it. Derek stays at the boat. She finds a shoe, holds it up, and puts it down exactly where she found it. She says all right, speaking only to herself. She marks the spot with a stick and photographs the shoe against the shoreline. No living person and no body are found.

That night they are back in the office. The tide charts hang as before; one chart is now marked in red. Derek is asleep in a chair. Maren is awake at the desk with a shoebox open, holding photographs, a bent railing bolt, and a plastic evidence bag that contains a shoe. She writes a date on the back of a photograph and puts the photograph into the box. Without opening his eyes, Derek tells her she has to sleep sometime. She says she sleeps. He says she does not. She closes the box and sets it on the shelf beside four identical boxes. The missing person is not recovered. Coastguard does not arrive inside the day. Derek does not change his position and does not become an antagonist; he remains in the chair, still telling her she will not rest. Maren does not name her grief and does not break. The only return from the search is the fifth box.
